source: Ma et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Can Be Effective Without Thinking
finding: At matched token budgets, skipping the long think phase (NoThinking) beats Thinking in low-budget settings, and the gap grows as more samples (k) are drawn. Closest test of acting on the quick first pass at equal tokens (gap 1).
numbers: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen, 7 datasets. AMC23 at 700 tokens: 51.3 vs 28.9. Under about 3,000 tokens NoThinking wins at every k; at about 3,500 tokens Thinking wins pass@1 but NoThinking passes from k=2. Matches Thinking with 3.3-3.7x fewer tokens on theorem proving. Parallel NoThinking plus best-of-N: up to 9x lower latency than sequential Thinking at similar accuracy.
quote: under a low-budget setting (e.g., fewer than 3,000 tokens), NoThinking consistently achieves better results than Thinking
limits: One model family (distilled R1). Pass@1 is worse at high budgets. On LiveCodeBench Thinking wins even at low budget. Not an RPD prompt: it removes thinking, it does not add recognise-then-simulate.
agent_relevance: Supports a cheap fast mode plus a parallel draw when a checker exists. Fast mode loses at high budget on hard single-shot tasks, so route by budget and checkability.

source: Brown et al. (2024) Large Language Monkeys: scaling inference compute with repeated sampling
finding: Coverage (any sample correct) grows log-linearly with the number of samples over four orders of magnitude when an automatic verifier exists. Without a verifier, majority vote and reward models plateau after several hundred samples.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite with DeepSeek-Coder-V2-Instruct: 15.9% with 1 sample to 56% with 250 samples, above the 43% single-sample state of the art.
quote: fraction of issues solved ... increases from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250 samples
limits: Gain depends on a verifier. Compute is many times that of one attempt, so this is not equal-token against a single deliberate try.
agent_relevance: Where a code-side check exists, many cheap candidates beat one careful candidate; supports generate-and-test over one-shot recognition (gap 1).

source: Snell et al. (2024) Scaling LLM test-time compute optimally can be more effective than scaling model parameters
finding: Which way to spend test-time compute depends on prompt difficulty. Easy prompts gain more from sequential revision; hard prompts gain more from parallel sampling or search. Matching strategy to difficulty beats plain best-of-N.
numbers: MATH, PaLM 2-S. Compute-optimal strategy matches best-of-N with about 4x less compute. FLOPs-matched: a smaller model with test-time compute can beat a 14x larger model on easy and intermediate questions, with little gain on the hardest. Beam search is worse than best-of-N on easy questions (levels 1-2) at high budget and better on levels 3-4. Sequential revisions narrowly beat parallel at equal samples; an ideal sequential-to-parallel ratio exists per budget.
quote: effectiveness of different approaches to scaling test-time compute critically varies depending on the difficulty of the prompt
limits: Needs a difficulty estimate (model-predicted difficulty costs compute and loses some of the gain). Math only. Trained revision model and process reward model, not prompting.
agent_relevance: A cheap router on estimated difficulty is a justified design (gap 3). Same logic as NDM: one fast pass when the case looks familiar, widen when it does not.

source: Chen et al. (2025) Do NOT think that much for 2+3=? On the overthinking of o1-like LLMs
finding: Reasoning models spend most tokens after the first correct solution. The first round already holds the correct answer in over 92 percent of cases, and it uses under 60 percent of tokens. Direct test of take-the-first for LLM output (gap 4).
numbers: On '2 plus 3': o1-like models used 1,953% more tokens than conventional models. First-correctness: more than 92% of cases first round correct; QwQ on ASDIV first round 287 tokens, 38.7% of the response; later rounds often repeat the same strategy (low diversity). Self-training to drop redundant rounds cut tokens 48.6% on MATH500 with accuracy kept.
quote: In more than 92% of cases, the initial round of solutions produces the correct answer.
limits: Only counts cases where some round is correct, so it shows later rounds add little, not that the first is always best. QwQ-32B-Preview and R1 only; math. Easy sets (ASDIV, GSM8K) dominate; harder sets may show lower first-round rates.
agent_relevance: On familiar tasks the first candidate is usually enough. Extra rounds should be triggered by a failed check, not run always (G1).

source: Chen et al. (2025) Overthinking: first-correct-solution (FCS) training variants
finding: Training on the first correct solution alone is most efficient but risks losing reflection; keeping a short second, different solution (FCS+Reflection) is the balanced choice.
numbers: Table 3 (QwQ-32B-Preview): shortest response 2.5 solutions, 1051.3 tokens; FCS 1.1 solutions, 878.7 tokens. Table 4 ASDIV: SimPO FCS+Reflection accuracy 96.9 with 3.5 solutions and 741.8 tokens in the printed row (column alignment in the text extract is ambiguous).
limits: Efficiency metrics are the authors' own. Gains are in token count; accuracy held roughly flat. Table text extraction was garbled, so treat the per-row numbers as approximate.
agent_relevance: Supports one candidate, then test; add a different second candidate only on failure. Diversity of strategy, not count, is what later rounds lacked.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large language models cannot self-correct reasoning yet
finding: Without an external signal, asking a model to review and correct its own answer does not help and often hurts. Gains reported earlier came from oracle labels telling the model when it was right. Relevant to gap 5: a critique pass run always can damage correct answers.
numbers: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 after round 1 and 41.8 after round 2; GSM8K 75.9 to 75.1 to 74.7. GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 to 89.0. With oracle labels GPT-4 GSM8K reaches 97.5 and HotpotQA 59.0. Self-consistency with 6 responses 85.3 and 9 responses 88.2 on GSM8K beat multi-agent debate with the same number of responses.
quote: LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction
limits: 2023 models (GPT-3.5, GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo, Llama-2). Prompt wording matters; later reasoning models may differ. CommonSenseQA drop is partly because wrong options look relevant.
agent_relevance: Do not run premortem or critique always. Trigger only on an external failed check, as G1 says.

source: Gema et al. (2025) Inverse scaling in test-time compute (controlled vs natural overthinking)
finding: Longer reasoning lowers accuracy on tasks with distractors, spurious features and constraint tracking. Failure types differ by model: Claude gets distracted; o-series resists distractors but overfits the framing.
numbers: Misleading Math and Misleading Python: 2,500 questions each, 500 per distractor count 1-5, true answer always 2. Claude Opus 4 in the controlled setup falls from near-perfect to about 80% on Python distractors with long reasoning. o3 stays stable or rises in the controlled setup but shows a weak inverse trend in the natural setup. DeepSeek R1 mostly flat. Few-shot examples largely fix the spurious-feature regression failure.
quote: extending the reasoning length of Large Reasoning Models (LRMs) deteriorates performance
limits: Tasks were built to expose the effect. Reasoning length is partly set by prompt, so confusion could drive both length and error (a public critique makes this point; seen only in a search snippet, not opened). Effect is model-specific.
agent_relevance: A token cap or think-briefly rule helps on distractor-heavy tasks; do not assume more thinking is safe. Few-shot exemplars help spurious-cue tasks (gap 7 partial).

source: Lee et al. (2026) Lost in the Noise: how reasoning models fail with contextual distractors (NoisyBench)
finding: Distractors in context cut accuracy by up to 80 percent in strong reasoning models, and more test-time compute makes it worse. Agent workflows over-trust noisy tool output. Prompting and context engineering did not fix it; a rationale-aware reward did.
numbers: 11 datasets over RAG, reasoning, alignment and tool use; up to 80% drop (Gemini-2.5-Pro among models). Inverse scaling with reasoning tokens in noisy settings (Appendix B.7).
quote: increased test-time computation leads to worse performance in noisy settings
limits: Fix is a training method, so it does not transfer to a scaffold-only agent. Drop sizes are maxima.
agent_relevance: Supports a short fast pass plus an explicit relevance filter on inputs; unlimited deliberation on a noisy context is a risk (gap 10).

source: Han et al. (2025) Token-budget-aware LLM reasoning (TALE)
finding: A token budget in the prompt compresses reasoning with little accuracy loss, if the budget is near the minimum needed. Too small a budget can raise cost or lower accuracy (token elasticity). Closest LLM analogue to time pressure (gap 10).
numbers: Averages over 6 sets with GPT-4o-mini: vanilla CoT 83.75% accuracy, 461.25 output tokens; TALE-EP 81.03%, 148.72 tokens (67% fewer tokens, under 3% accuracy loss). A fixed tiny budget of 5 tokens: 52.31% average accuracy. Token elasticity: budgets below the optimum can cost more tokens than a larger one.
limits: Mostly arithmetic and math word problems; the budget is set by an estimator. Not a stress effect: models do not get worse in a human sense, they get shorter.
agent_relevance: Token caps do not copy human stress degradation; they trade accuracy for length smoothly until a floor. Pair a cap with a failed-check escape.

source: Muennighoff et al. (2025) s1: simple test-time scaling (budget forcing)
finding: Forcing the model to stop thinking, or appending Wait to extend it, controls test-time compute; accuracy rises with more thinking within a range.
numbers: s1-32B from 1,000 training examples exceeds o1-preview by up to 27% on competition math; AIME24 from 50% to 57% with budget forcing extrapolation.
limits: Fine-tuned model; math. Only the abstract and introduction were read in detail.
agent_relevance: Shows both a cap and an extension lever exist. Cap on easy items, extend on failed checks.

source: Dhuliawala et al. (2023) Chain-of-Verification reduces hallucination
finding: Draft, plan verification questions, answer them independently, then revise. Factored versions (verification answered without seeing the draft) beat the joint one. Nearest published LLM analogue to a data-frame or premortem check (gap 5).
numbers: Llama 65B Wikidata list questions, precision: few-shot 0.17, CoVe joint 0.29, factored 0.32, two-step 0.36 (more than doubles). Longform biography FACTSCORE rises from 0.39 to 0.48 for the best variant per the text.
limits: Always-on pipeline; trigger-only vs always-on not compared. Fact recall tasks, not decisions. Not a premortem. Table text extraction is garbled for some rows.
agent_relevance: Independence of the check from the draft matters; a premortem prompt should not see the plan's rationale. Trigger comparison remains untested (gap 5 open).

source: Frontiers 2016 perspective citing Klein, Calderwood and Clinton-Cirocco (1986)
finding: Page read this session. It gives the 80-90 percent figure and the Proceedings citation (Human Factors Society, vol. 30, pp. 576-580) but not the number of commanders, decisions or the coding rules.
numbers: 80-90% of firefighters' decisions attributed to RPD (Klein 1986 and Klein 1989 together).
limits: Secondary source. The DTIC full text (ADA199492) returned a damaged file and the citation page returned 403, so the 1986 counts remain unchecked (gap 6 open).
agent_relevance: Keep the 80-90 percent figure labelled secondary in the notes.

finding: Page lists settings (trauma nurses, fireground commanders, chess players, stock traders) and cites Klein 1998 pp. 1-30. It has no 1986 counts or coding.
agent_relevance: Nothing new; do not cite it for the percentage.

source: Gap 3 synthesis: difficulty-based routing across Snell, Chen and Han
finding: Three independent LLM papers support routing on estimated difficulty: Snell (easy: revise; hard: search), Chen (first round enough on easy sets), Han (budget scaled to complexity). Liu et al. archetypes (implicit pattern, visual) predict where explicit reasoning hurts; no paper read tested a cheap router on those archetypes.
numbers: Snell: about 4x compute saving; Chen: 48.6% token cut; Han: 67% token cut with under 3% accuracy loss.
limits: This line is my synthesis of papers I read, not a new source. Difficulty estimates cost compute (Snell: gain shrinks with predicted vs oracle difficulty). No router tested on pattern-vs-deliberate archetypes.
agent_relevance: Build the router on checks available cheaply (does a verifier exist, is the task pattern-like), then test it. Status: partly supported, untested for archetypes.
